figures.title: The n × n score matrix is the quadratic term
figures.caption: Every query scores every key, so the score matrix is n × n; the causal mask keeps the lower triangle. At n = 131,072, n² = 1.718 × 10^10 entries. The chapter rounds that to 10^10 entries, so at 2 bytes each one head in one layer is 20 GB, about 10.4 percent of the 192 GB of HBM on an H100, and the product over heads and layers passes the budget many times over. The grid is a schematic 10 × 10; the numbers are the chapter's.
figures.alt: A 10 by 10 causal score grid. Filled cells are allowed query-key pairs with j ≤ i; the upper triangle is masked. Row 8 is highlighted. The note gives n = 131,072, n² = 1.718 × 10^10 entries, and 20 GB per head per layer in fp16 once the count is rounded to 10^10.

data.note: Schematic 10 × 10 causal grid, not to scale: the lower triangle holds 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 of the 100 cells. At n = 131,072 the matrix has n² = 1.718 × 10^10 entries; the causal triangle has n(n+1)/2. Rounding to 10^10 entries at 2 bytes per fp16 entry, one head in one layer is 20 GB, about 10.4 percent of the 192 GB of HBM on an H100; all heads and layers pass that budget many times over.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to fill the causal triangle row by row, then price it.

steps.label: Query i scores every key j ≤ i: rows 0 and 1 hold 1 + 2 = 3 cells.
Rows 8 and 9 hold 9 + 10 = 19, so the triangle totals 3 + 12 + 21 + 19 = 55 of the 100 cells: n(n+1)/2.

The upper triangle j > i is masked and never computed, so the bound is n² = 1.718 × 10^10 at n = 131,072; at 2 bytes per fp16 entry that is 20 GB for one head in one layer, 20 / 192 = 0.104 of the 192 GB on an H100.

figures.title: Quadratic and linear attention on log-log axes
figures.caption: On log-log axes, quadratic attention rises with slope 2 and linear attention with slope 1. The plotted points run from n = 128 to n = 2048 and are relative costs computed from n/128, an illustrative normalization; the chapter's absolute counts at n = 131,072 are in the note. At n = 4096 the quadratic cost is 1024× the n = 128 cost and linear is 32×. The crossover at n = d = 128 is where linear attention becomes cheaper.
figures.alt: A log-log plot. The horizontal axis is sequence length n from 1 to 10,000; the vertical axis is cost relative to n = 128 from 1 to 1,000. The quadratic line passes through (128, 1), (256, 4), (512, 16), (1024, 64) and (2048, 256); the linear line passes through (128, 1), (256, 2), (512, 4), (1024, 8) and (2048, 16). The quadratic line is twice as steep.

data.note: Relative cost is illustrative: quadratic attention scales as (n/128)², linear attention as n/128; the crossover is at n = d = 128, which the chapter states. At n = 4096 the quadratic ratio is 1024 and the linear ratio is 32. Absolute figures at n = 131,072: 1.718 × 10^10 score entries; 2.199 × 10^12 multiply-adds for the scores per head per layer, and the same again for value aggregation, so 4.40 × 10^12; a 4,096-token window cuts entries to 536,870,912, 32× fewer; linear attention costs 2,147,483,648 operations.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to compare the two slopes on log-log axes.

steps.label: Quadratic attention costs (n/128)², so the line rises with slope 2.
Linear attention costs n/128, slope 1: at n = 4096 the ratios are 1024 and 32.
The two meet at n = d = 128; past that point linear attention is the cheaper form.

sources.note: Dao et al., FlashAttention; tiled softmax and the running maximum and sum.
Katharopoulos et al., Transformers are RNNs; linear attention and the O(n d²) cost.
Child et al., Sparse Transformer; the windowed mask that cuts the n² entries.
